project_name: BioValue AI demo: fictional softwood kraft lignin stream
disclaimers: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.
BioValue AI gives indicative decision support. It does not guarantee profitability, does not verify customer demand, and does not constitute engineering approval.

Gross margin, profitability, NPV, and IRR are not calculated. They need capital costs, fixed costs, a discount rate, a time horizon, and agreed definitions, none of which are available yet. Gross contribution excludes capital costs, fixed costs, and the value of the feedstock in its current use.
Scores use a 1-5 scale. A criterion that was not assessed lowers data completeness; it is never counted as a low score.

constraints: The stream is currently fired as internal fuel, so diverting it to external sales would affect the mill's existing fuel-use route.
The lignin leaves the mill as wet cake at the recorded moisture, and no lignin dryer is available; buyers needing dry powder would need drying before use.
Covered cake storage is limited, so wet-cake storage and shipment would constrain operations.
Solvent or membrane fractionation is not available, limiting uses that require fractionated lignin.
Chemical modification equipment is not available, limiting uses that require modified lignin.
Ash, molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium are missing, limiting confirmation against buyer or pathway specifications.
The reported lignin-content method is unclear, so comparisons with specifications require method confirmation.
Moisture is uncertain, affecting dry tonnage and shipped mass.
data_quality_notes: This is fictional demo data, not measured data from a real mill; all figures are illustrative assumptions and must be replaced with mill lab data and production records before decisions.
The recorded data status is fictional_demo, so results say nothing about a real mill.
The validation confirmed the dry-matter balance but did not check the composition total because ash is missing.
The reported lignin-content analytical method is stated for illustration only and should be confirmed before comparison with buyer specifications.
Moisture is identified as uncertain and should be measured over operating conditions before relying on the dry-mass profile.
agent.summary: Validated fictional softwood kraft lignin filter-cake profile: 40000.0 t/yr wet mass, moisture fraction 0.35000000000000003, and 26000.0 t/yr dry mass; no contradictions were found, but four composition fields are missing and the data are unsuitable for real-world decisions until replaced with measured mill data.

lignin_pct.method: Acid-insoluble (Klason) plus acid-soluble lignin, as % of dry matter (method stated for illustration)

sulfur_pct.method: Total sulfur by elemental analysis (stated for illustration)

carbohydrates_pct.method: Total sugars after acid hydrolysis (stated for illustration)

checks.disclaimer: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.

current_use.description: Fictional: the precipitated lignin is fired in the mill's own boilers in place of purchased fuel. The unit was built to relieve the recovery boiler, not to sell lignin.

geographic_market.logistics: Fictional: rail siding at the mill; the nearest deep-water port is assumed to be about 150 km away.

supported_claims.EV-PF-01#1: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#2: UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#4: Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#2: Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#R1: Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-04#2: With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#3: A 2018 report cited by the IEA estimates the technology readiness level (TRL) for producing biobased phenolic resins at 8.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin can partially replace phenol in phenol-formaldehyde resins, with a typical replacement of up to 50% when using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin.
Lignin-phenol-formaldehyde resin is supported for plywood and other wood-based-panel adhesives; UPM reports LPF resin meeting veneer-plywood Bonding Class 3.

target_customers.statement: Potential customer types include plywood manufacturers and producers of other wood-based panels that use phenol-formaldehyde adhesives.

competing_materials.statement: The incumbent material is phenol used in phenol-formaldehyde resins.

qualification_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin needs activation or depolymerization before use in phenol-formaldehyde resins.
A plywood LPF-resin application is reported to meet EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
One laboratory study assessed viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde against the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in that study.

limitations: The strongest market-scale figures are from a review and include a forecast with no year attached; the market value is from 2019.
The UPM performance and cost claims are vendor technical literature without a cited test report, and the document does not state that its lignin is kraft lignin.
The laboratory resin study used poplar plywood samples and reports the applicable standard inconsistently.

The feedstock lacks ash, molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl, and sodium data, and has no chemical-modification equipment; this limits confirmation that the stream meets pathway specifications and the stated pretreatment requirement.
missing_information: No lignin purchase price, delivered price, annual demand volume, named buyer, contract terms, or regional demand is provided.
The evidence does not establish whether a buyer would accept this wet cake, and the feedstock has no dryer while dry-powder users would need drying.
The evidence does not provide a commercial process design or cost for activation or depolymerization of this stream.
The feedstock is fictional demo data and requires measured mill data before commercial decisions.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence shows industrially proven LPF resin and a documented plywood qualification claim, while the broader literature reports high readiness and substantial PF-resin use. However, it does not document named buyers or commercial sales by multiple producers, so it supports documented industry development rather than the highest market-evidence levels.

supported_claims.EV-PU-01#1: Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#1: Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#3: Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
supported_claims.EV-PU-02#1: Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#1: The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#2: In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#R1: Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#R1: Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
supported_claims.EV-PU-05#1: Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

applications.statement: Lignin is supported as a partial replacement for petroleum-based polyols in rigid polyurethane/polyisocyanurate foams; in one study, replacing 30 wt% of petroleum polyol with unmodified lignin produced foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications for 16 of 19 lignins tested.

Kraft lignin has been studied in flexible polyurethane foam at a 20 wt% replacement of petroleum-based polyol; the authors suggest kraft-lignin foams may suit heavy-duty foam applications because they were denser and stiffer.
Kraft lignin has been reported in rigid foams at 19-23% of finished-foam mass while maintaining comparable structure and strength in the cited study.

target_customers.statement: Potential customer types include rigid-foam producers, insulation-foam producers, flexible-foam producers, and users of heavy-duty foam.

competing_materials.statement: The incumbent material is petroleum-based polyol.

qualification_requirements.statement: The cited acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production is total hydroxyl value above 200 mg KOH/g, equivalent to 3.56 mmol/g total OH; this is total OH rather than phenolic OH.
One rigid-foam study evaluated performance against ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Kraft lignin generally needs significant treatment, such as oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction, to reach target polyurethane properties.

limitations: Most evidence is laboratory foam work; the rigid-foam study does not give a kraft-only pass rate and the best performer was an enzymatic-hydrolysis lignin.
Reported replacement levels come from individual studies and are not general limits; lignin can lower compressive strength, resiliency, elongation, or increase viscosity.
A review rates polyurethane lignin uses at TRL 6 for a broad row covering foams, panels, coatings, and rubber replacement, not kraft-lignin foam specifically.
The evidence includes a moderate-quality abstract-only review that identifies consistency, performance, and cost as commercialization barriers.
The feedstock has no chemical-modification equipment, and its missing hydroxyl, molecular-weight, ash, and sodium data limit pathway qualification; it is also wet cake without a dryer.
missing_information: No lignin price, polyurethane-grade sales volume, named buyer, customer trial, contract, or regional demand is provided.
The evidence does not establish whether the stream's total hydroxyl value, viscosity, ash, odor, or other properties meet a specific buyer formulation.
The evidence does not provide the cost or process design for required lignin modification.
The evidence does not identify a commercial sales channel for this particular kraft-lignin stream.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence shows research demonstrations and a broad TRL-6 assessment, but it does not document a named buyer, development partnership, pilot with a customer, or commercial sale of lignin-based polyurethane material.

supported_claims.EV-CM-02#3: Softwood lignin gives high carbon yields (55% or more) but is not readily melt-spinnable without a plasticizing agent; hardwood lignin is the reverse, with slightly lower yield (50-55%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#2: Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#1: Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#3: Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#1: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#1: DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#1: A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R1: Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R2: Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R3: Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R4: Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R5: Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R1: Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R2: Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#R1: Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#1: Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#1: The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#2: Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.

applications.statement: The pathway supports carbon fiber precursor development, with softwood lignin identified as providing carbon yields of 55% or more; however, softwood lignin is not readily melt-spinnable without a plasticizing agent.

Kraft lignin is supported as a precursor for hard carbon for sodium-ion battery anodes; a review reports higher initial coulombic efficiency for hard carbon made from kraft lignin than for hard carbon made from sulfonated lignin, attributing the difference to lower ash content.
Lignin can be converted to activated carbon even when it is too impure for other carbon-material uses, and lower ash improves activated-carbon yield and carbon conversion.

target_customers.statement: Potential customer types include carbon-fiber precursor and carbon-fiber producers, sodium-ion battery-anode-material producers, and activated-carbon producers.

competing_materials.statement: The named competing materials are PAN-based carbon fiber, anthracite or pitch for hard carbon, and conventional activated carbon.

qualification_requirements.statement: The cited ORNL carbon-fiber precursor specifications include lignin content greater than 99%, ash below 0.1% by weight, volatile material below 5% at 250 °C, residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm, and removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
The kraft lignin examined for carbon fiber needed purification, and softwood lignin needs a plasticizing or alloying agent for melt spinning.
Activated carbon has no strict precursor-quality limitation in the cited study, although lower ash improves yield.
Battery-material qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years according to Stora Enso.

limitations: The carbon-fiber specifications are for the most demanding carbon material and do not apply directly to hard carbon or activated carbon; they are also cited secondhand from ORNL work.
The carbon-fiber study used lignin from a near-neutral hemicellulose-extraction process rather than standard kraft pulping, and the DOE work dates to the FY2009 program.
The GreenLight evidence is a project summary with modelled costs; its TRL 5 applies to precursor-fiber spinning, not the whole lignin-to-carbon-fiber chain.
The hard-carbon evidence is a review covering sodium-ion batteries, while the battery pilot evidence concerns lithium-ion batteries and provides no lignin quality specifications.
The activated-carbon study was laboratory work using zinc chloride activation.

The feedstock has missing ash and other composition data, no fractionation equipment, and wet-cake handling and storage constraints; the carbon-fiber ash specification cannot be checked against the profile.
missing_information: No named buyer, purchase agreement, qualified product sale, regional demand, or customer-specific specification is provided for this stream.
No measured ash, molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl, sodium, volatile content, particulate distribution, or residual-carbohydrate result is provided.
No cost, equipment design, yield for this feedstock, or energy requirement is provided for purification, spinning, carbonization, battery-anode production, or activation.
The evidence does not establish whether the relevant opportunity is sodium-ion or lithium-ion battery material for a prospective customer.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents industrially relevant carbon-fiber precursor development, a project with precursor-fiber TRL 5, and battery qualification partnerships and pilot-scale activity. It does not document commercial sales by a lignin producer or several established buyers, so the evidence is stronger than research-only interest but below commercial-market levels.

processing_requirements.statement: The mill would need activation or depolymerization before its kraft lignin could be used in phenol-formaldehyde resins.
A commercial route would also need to address the mill's lack of chemical-modification equipment, wet-cake form, limited covered storage, and competition with the existing internal-fuel route.

technical_maturity.statement: Biobased phenolic-resin production is reported at TRL 8, although that rating is for biobased phenolic resins generally rather than this kraft-lignin stream specifically.

adoption_barriers.statement: Customers would need qualification evidence for resin viscosity, bonding strength, free formaldehyde, and plywood performance; the cited evidence includes a Bonding Class 3 claim but does not establish acceptance of this stream.
The pathway competes with phenol and lacks a named buyer, purchase terms, regional demand, or evidence that a customer would accept wet cake.
The feedstock's ash, molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, sodium, analytical-method basis, and measured moisture remain unresolved for specification and logistics decisions.

assumptions: The economics tool used fictional wet-feedstock assumptions of 36000.0, 40000.0, and 43000.0 t/yr for the conservative, base, and optimistic cases, respectively.
The economics tool used fictional moisture assumptions of 40.0%, 35.0%, and 30.0% of wet mass, respectively.
The economics tool used fictional availability fractions of 40.0%, 50.0%, and 60.0%, respectively.

The economics tool calculated dry mass and usable dry feedstock only; product output, revenue, variable cost, and gross contribution were not calculated because product yield, product price, and variable costs were missing.
The pathway feasibility score is a judgment under the supplied rubric: 2, because activation or depolymerization and drying or a buyer-compatible wet-cake route are not existing mill capabilities.
uncertainties: Feedstock compatibility was not scored because the evidence library supplied no numeric requirements for this pathway.
Indicative economics were not scored because product yield, product price, and variable costs were missing; profitability, NPV, and IRR were also not calculated.
The TRL evidence covers biobased phenolic resins generally, not necessarily kraft lignin from this mill.
The feedstock is fictional demo data, and moisture and composition measurements may materially change qualification and logistics decisions.

commercialization_feasibility.rationale: The pathway has a relatively mature general technology base, but this mill lacks the chemical-modification capability needed for the kraft-lignin route and lacks drying capability for dry-powder customers. Commercialization therefore needs major new processing capability and an identified partner or buyer.

feedstock_compatibility.rationale: The evidence library has no numeric requirements for this pathway to check against.

technical_readiness.rationale: TRL 8 maps to 5. Stated in EV-PF-01#3.

indicative_economics.rationale: Gross contribution per tonne could not be calculated. Missing inputs: product yield, product price, variable costs.

processing_requirements.statement: For carbon-fiber precursor production, the lignin would need purification, removal of particulates larger than 1 µm, and a plasticizing or alloying agent for melt spinning of softwood lignin.
The cited carbon-fiber precursor specifications include lignin content greater than 99% and ash below 0.1% by weight, while this profile reports lignin content of 94 and does not report ash.
Activated-carbon production is a less specification-intensive subroute in the cited evidence, but it still requires process development and activation equipment not described for this mill.

technical_maturity.statement: The GreenLight project raised lignin precursor-fiber production to TRL 5 in an industrially relevant environment, but that rating covers precursor-fiber spinning rather than the complete lignin-to-carbon-fiber chain.

adoption_barriers.statement: The pathway spans distinct markets—carbon-fiber precursors, sodium-ion battery anodes, and activated carbon—with different specifications, processing routes, and customer qualification requirements.

Carbon-fiber qualification is especially constrained because the cited precursor specification requires lignin content greater than 99% and ash below 0.1% by weight, while ash and other relevant quality results are missing.
Battery-material qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and no named buyer, agreement, qualified sale, or customer-specific specification is provided.

Wet-cake handling, limited covered storage, absent fractionation equipment, and missing ash, molecular-weight, phenolic-OH, sodium, volatile, particulate, and residual-carbohydrate data constrain route selection and qualification.

report.summary: Carbon materials are the only pathway ranked by the scoring engine and are ranked first, with attractiveness 3.13 and a range of 2.7–3.5. Phenolic resins show higher assessed attractiveness at 3.45, but remain insufficient-data because feedstock compatibility and economics were not assessed. Polyurethanes are also insufficient-data, with assessed attractiveness 2.36. The next decision should prioritize measured feedstock characterization, route-specific buyer specifications, economic inputs, and customer or technology-partner validation rather than treating the current order as a final investment recommendation.

documented_facts.statement: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
A 2018 report cited by the IEA estimates the technology readiness level (TRL) for producing biobased phenolic resins at 8.
Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.

Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.
Softwood lignin gives high carbon yields (55% or more) but is not readily melt-spinnable without a plasticizing agent; hardwood lignin is the reverse, with slightly lower yield (50-55%).
Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.

Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
